title: How to View Teaching Situations Where the Odds are Against You: A Personal Case Study
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Using his first-ever AP World History class, open only to ninth graders, as a case study, Stuart contrasts two ways teachers interpret hard situations: problem-as-conclusive and problem-as-opportunity. He first honestly lists the reasons the problem-as-conclusive stance is tempting, including College Board warnings, brain development, extra time demands and fear of looking bad. He then argues that asking how the obstacle might be an opportunity improves both quality of life and performance. His breakthroughs were that ninth graders have more free time, that being the underdog is motivating, and that failing at something hard may be a formative first experience. He adds that teachers should still advocate against genuinely fixable bad conditions such as 40-plus-student classes, and calls this reframing the inner work of teaching.
points: Teachers' interpretations of hard situations tend to split into problem-as-conclusive (the problem is the final word) and problem-as-opportunity.
Stuart models honest first-draft thinking, showing how a weak Why not? answer had to be revised before it could stand up to scrutiny.
Concrete opportunities he found: ninth graders have more time, underdog status motivates, and the course gives many students their first drowning academic experience.
He separates reframing from resignation by insisting that fixable problems like oversized classes or divisive leadership should still be organized against.
He defends the AP exam as a different kind of test from state high-stakes accountability tests, giving students financial benefit and well-founded confidence.
quotes: Every single year in the classroom — heck, every single day — presents challenging situations that demand our interpretation. The class with the higher-than-usual number of IEPs; the teaching schedule with four different preps; the chronic behavioral outbursts from fourth period; the divisive district leadership: we can't not interpret situations like this.

Basically, Problem-as-Opportunity requires that we re-examine our chief obstacle from a creative standpoint. Rather than accepting the instinctual Problem-as-Conclusive thoughts that anyone can produce, we ask “How might this actually be an opportunity?” We keep doing that until we arrive someplace helpful.
First, I realized that ninth graders have more time than upperclassmen. Most don't have varsity sports, jobs, intense club responsibilities, or competing college-level classes.
Then, I realized that it's motivating being the underdog. I started showing my students statistics about how poorly ninth graders do on the APWH test.

Once we were a few months in, many students admitted to this being their first “Oh my goodness, I'm drowning” academic experience. How huge is that? What a privilege to be able to give that first experience to my kids.

We should advocate and organize against fixable situations that are bad for kids. 40+ students per Spanish class is a problem; it may please the eye of the person looking at the school budget spreadsheet, but it's ultimately bad for kids.
This allows us to grow and perform in ways we otherwise wouldn't; it also allows us to find true joy in the midst of the struggle. This is the inner work of teaching. This matters, a lot.
